fields.question: How prevent future leakage in SIM top-k history?
fields.answer: GSU searches only pre-request history, separate from the target label. ESU sees selected entries only. MovieLens verifies mechanism, not production or online A/B.
fields.example: Do not add the next actual click before searching history.

fields.question: Why use GSU then ESU instead of scoring lifelong history directly?
fields.answer: Most history is irrelevant per candidate. Cheap GSU narrows it, then ESU attends precisely to selected behavior. Fine matching cannot recover evidence omitted by coarse retrieval.
fields.example: If category filtering excludes old lens interactions, later camera attention cannot see them.

fields.question: Why train on both triggers and exemptions in SIRF?
fields.answer: Safety decisions depend on exceptions as well as triggers. Synthetic rules and continued pretraining aim to cover rare combinations; thresholds manage precision.
fields.example: A keyword need not violate policy in an explicitly exempt explanatory context.

fields.question: How does learned rule internalization differ from a runtime rules engine?
fields.answer: Learned models can generalize language and context but need not obey every rule exactly. Explicit engines obey coded conditions with limited coverage. Accuracy is not formal proof.
fields.example: A model may retain an old policy after the rule changes.

fields.question: Does the local high-precision threshold reproduce full 8B continued pretraining?
fields.answer: No. It uses trigger/exemption proxies, not private accounts, EntiGraph/MAGA generation, or large training. Select thresholds on validation and keep held-out reporting separate.
fields.example: A small classifier reaching precision target does not reproduce a safety foundation model.

fields.question: Why train synthetic trigger/exemption rules and threshold one verdict?
fields.answer: Long-tail combinations are scarce in logs. Rule graphs, rewrites, and account reasoning teach combinations during continued pretraining; one verdict saves online work. Threshold trades precision and recall. Local interactions are not production capability.
fields.example: Frequent trades can trigger concern, but verified merchant status may exempt them.

fields.question: Why use both shared and private experts in SMES?
fields.answer: Stable shared experts hold common signals, task-private experts preserve differences, and global load balances cross-task dispatch.
fields.example: Viewing and buying share interest features but can retain distinct decision experts.

fields.question: How do shared/private pools differ from one MoE router?
fields.answer: Separate pools constrain common and task-specific selections; one pool lets all compete. This does not guarantee less negative transfer.
fields.example: Reserving all shared capacity for purchases can harm other tasks.

fields.question: Can balancing be computed separately per task only?
fields.answer: No. Separate balance can miss aggregate expert overload. Use cross-task counts. MovieLens lacks production sparse scheduling, so dispatch counts are not throughput.
fields.example: Individually spread tasks can all favor the same two experts globally.

fields.question: Why combine fixed shared activation, adaptive private experts, and global balance?
fields.answer: Shared capacity handles commonality, private routing handles task differences, and global balance detects concentration hidden within tasks. Actual specialization and balance penalties still require evaluation.
fields.example: Clicks and purchases can share interest experts while choosing novelty or price specialists, unless global dispatch overloads one.

fields.question: Why compress intent rather than equate clicks with Snap DPA relevance?
fields.answer: Clicks are sparse and exposure-biased. Group recent behavior by SID and event type, then apply business-aligned relevance criteria. This is a separate demand metric, not renamed CTR.
fields.example: Repeated recent cart additions can be stronger intent evidence than one exposure.

fields.question: Why can MicroRel and MacroRel disagree?
fields.answer: Micro averages user–candidate pairs, while macro weights users equally. Users with many candidates dominate micro more. Report both rather than cherry-pick.
fields.example: Active users with many candidates affect micro disproportionately.

fields.question: Can gold relevance labels stand in for detector predictions?
fields.answer: No. Train a real detector on discovered, human-reviewed business criteria and evaluate independently. Rule discovery has bootstrap and per-class F1 requirements; coverage review cannot be skipped.
fields.example: Copying gold computes a score without learning relevance.

fields.question: Why distinguish MicroRel and MacroRel and vet criteria first?
fields.answer: Compressed history supplies intent; a criteria-trained detector judges candidates. Pair-level and user-level averages answer different questions, but neither repairs wrong relevance judgments. Private review and commercial model workflows are not reproduced.
fields.example: With 100 and ten candidates, user one weighs ten times as much in micro but equally in macro.

fields.question: Why build a co-engagement graph before SnapLGR SIDs?
fields.answer: Propagation adds collaborative relationships, residual quantization turns them into hierarchical paths, and generation predicts codes from history. Behavior complements content.
fields.example: Visually different items consumed by one audience can become connected.

fields.question: What does grounding SID tokens add beyond discrete-code likelihood?
fields.answer: Alignment preserves content meaning instead of learning only code transitions. Its benefit depends on embedding and graph quality, not any arbitrary semantic code.
fields.example: Related videos' code representations should reflect their content relationship.

fields.question: What behavior can graph propagation and quantization use?
fields.answer: Only allowed training co-engagement, without future test edges. Pin codebook and mapping versions. Public features do not reproduce Snap logs, scale, or traffic.
fields.example: Test clicks in the graph leak retrieval relationships.

fields.question: Why propagate co-engagement, quantize, then ground generated tokens?
fields.answer: Graphs add collaborative signals, quantization encodes them in discrete paths, grounding ties codes back to content, and next-SID prediction learns transitions. Popularity bias can propagate too.
fields.example: Visually different co-consumed items can become neighbors, but codes still must resolve reliably to relevant content.

fields.question: Why predict future user–item pairs before computing SOLARIS latents?
fields.answer: Computing all pairs online is expensive. Predict likely pairs and asynchronously precompute them for lightweight consumption. Misses need fallback and wrong guesses waste budget.
fields.example: Prepare representations for a shortlist instead of an entire catalog.

fields.question: How does a latent cache differ from a final list cache?
fields.answer: A latent is a middle feature the lightweight ranker can combine with current inputs. A cached list fixes ordering. Latents still age and need version consistency.
fields.example: Reusing a latent with today's price can change yesterday's order.

fields.question: What should a SOLARIS cache key capture?
fields.answer: User/item identity, model and feature versions, and validity; define hit and fallback paths. An abstract implementation or hit rate does not prove service latency.
fields.example: Do not silently reuse a latent from a previous model version.

fields.question: Why cache predicted pair latents instead of one user vector?
fields.answer: Deep interactions depend on a particular item. Predict likely pairs, compute asynchronously, use hits and fallback on misses. Coverage, freshness, and budget matter. Future outcomes can supervise training, not online selection.
fields.example: Precompute ten likely products, but serve an unexpected one through fallback.

fields.question: Why use both SID generation and ranking in Sona?
fields.answer: Share user state across candidate generation and fine ranking instead of duplicating representations. A large teacher guides training only; one model serves.
fields.example: Generate songs and score specific songs from the same user state.

fields.question: How does a unified model differ from deleting an intermediate ranker?
fields.answer: Joint generation, ranking, and distillation must replace functionality and handle long history. Compare coverage and robustness; fewer models alone do not prove improvement.
fields.example: Dropping pre-ranking without joint training can just remove functionality.

fields.question: Does Sona call its teacher at serving?
fields.answer: No. Teacher is training-only. Local work omits the full teacher, music tokenizer, and 15-plus-source production stack. Generation/ranking losses share state with distinct masks.
fields.example: Calling the large teacher online changes the cost contract.
